title: Knowledge Within Reach
coreMove: Watch how the arms manage distance: what they block, protect, offer, contain, or reach toward.
sourcePressure: The source sidecar says support is thinner here, so claims must stay concrete: arm barriers, reach, tucked arms, folded arms, protective holding, invitation, restraint, and visible distance management. The chapter must not turn folded arms into automatic defensiveness.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version treats arms as a generic attitude signal. The writer must make arms specific by showing what they put between the person and the moment, what they hold close, and what they make available.

hook: A generic office meeting where everyone crosses their arms.
A hostility frame built from one arm position.
counterintuition: Most people assume folded arms mean defensiveness, but actually...
Arm barriers reveal the person's true attitude.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and watch crossed arms.
Uncross your arms to seem approachable.
Mirror another person's arms to create trust.
examples: Romantic attraction or rejection by arm angle.

exampleSpecs.domain: airport lost-luggage counter during a delayed baggage claim
exampleSpecs.audience: a baggage supervisor deciding whether to press for more forms or create space for a frustrated traveler
exampleSpecs.stakes: the conversation can stay procedural if the supervisor reads the arm barrier before the traveler raises his voice
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The traveler says he is fine filling out the claim, but hugs the garment bag across his chest, pins the baggage tag under one elbow, and keeps the other forearm on the counter edge like a gate.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A torn baggage tag is trapped beneath a forearm on the claim counter.

exampleSpecs.domain: blood donation intake after a first-time donor sees the needle tray
exampleSpecs.audience: a phlebotomist watching whether the donor needs a slower explanation
exampleSpecs.stakes: pushing too quickly could make the donor withdraw before the screening is complete
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The donor keeps saying let's do it, but one arm clamps over the donation packet while the other hand reaches only halfway toward the consent pen, so the phlebotomist moves the needle tray out of the direct line of sight.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A capped consent pen lies beside a sealed needle tray.

exampleSpecs.domain: vinyl record store listening booth during a rare-album negotiation
exampleSpecs.audience: a shop owner trying to tell whether a collector is protecting the item or inviting a deal
exampleSpecs.stakes: the wrong read could turn a possible sale into a guarded standoff
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: When the price comes up, the collector pulls the sleeve tight under both forearms; when the owner mentions a store-credit option, one arm releases and slides the sleeve halfway across the counter.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A rare blue-label record sleeve rests below a listening-booth speaker.
mustAvoid: one reach as proof of agreement

exampleSpecs.domain: community swimming lesson where a parent hands off a toddler
exampleSpecs.audience: a swim instructor judging whether to take the child yet or keep the parent involved
exampleSpecs.stakes: a rushed handoff can make the child cling harder and sour the first lesson
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the handoff, the parent cradles the toddler with both arms locked high; after the instructor offers a floating toy, one arm lowers toward the water and leaves a clear path between child and pool.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A yellow floating toy bumps against the tiled pool edge.

exampleSpecs.domain: bike repair co-op explaining a brake adjustment to a new rider
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer mechanic deciding whether to keep demonstrating or hand over the tool
exampleSpecs.stakes: the rider needs enough ownership to ride safely, but too much pressure will make him retreat
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The mechanic predicts the rider is not ready while both arms stay tucked around the frame; when the rider reaches past the cable housing and rests one forearm on the work stand, the mechanic offers the hex key.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A loose brake cable arcs above a silver work stand.

exampleSpecs.domain: library makerspace soldering orientation before open lab
exampleSpecs.audience: a librarian watching whether a patron is ready to handle equipment
exampleSpecs.stakes: safety depends on noticing restraint before the iron is placed in someone's hand
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: On review, the librarian sees the patron kept both elbows pinned to her sides during the heat warning, then extended only one forearm toward the spool after the librarian placed the iron back in its stand.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A soldering iron rests in a ceramic stand beside a coil of silver wire.
mustAvoid: hand-tremor focus that belongs in chapter 7

skillTargets: identify arms as barriers, invitations, protective holds, restraint, or reach in concrete scenes
separate arm-based distance management from hostility, deception, attitude, or personality claims
choose a next move that adjusts space, object placement, or pace based on arm behavior
evaluate when folded or tucked arms are explained by temperature, task, safety, habit, or object handling

tryThisNowSpec: During one exchange today, notice what your arms are doing with space: guarding an object, holding yourself in, offering something forward, or keeping a boundary. Name only the distance move.
